Odin in Godot

The onboarding series

2 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓

This series shows how to write Godot gameplay in compiled Odin and organize shared state for multiplayer. It assumes you know scenes, nodes, callbacks, and ordinary game development; it introduces the Odin and Kit conventions as they appear.

Read the posts in order: each introduces a mechanism used by the next. Keep the Authoring Guide open for API details, and use Build a game in a day for a step-by-step project.

  1. Writing compiled Godot scripts covers the scene workflow, the compile step, and the script layout. It ends with a moving node.
  2. Thinking in structs maps the script conventions. Each GDScript feature (@export, @onready, signals, inheritance, autoloads) maps to an Odin convention or an explicit alternative. It also distinguishes the script struct (self) from the engine node (self.owner).
  3. Field replication introduces the multiplayer model: declare which fields replicate and which peer writes them. It builds a hosted session from declared scenes, handlers, and a ready() setup call.
  4. Predicted commands treats player actions as predicted commands. The generated pipeline handles submission and rejection; the command supplies the game-specific validation and target mutation.
  5. The two timelines explains why local and remote screens show different moments, and how to schedule an effect beside its visible cause.
  6. Identity, recovery, and transport testing covers persistent identity, drop-in joins, saves, host migration, and Steam, including the setup and integration tests those features need.
  7. Server-authoritative simulation moves motion authority to the server. It introduces local input prediction, correction, and presentation for contested objects, using three versions of a soccer game.

Posts 1–6 cover cooperative replication; post 7 adds server-authoritative simulation. Both use field declarations to select the state policy, so a game can combine a cooperative lobby with server-authoritative hitboxes. The references are kit/sim (the full lane) and timelines (the per-field choosing guide).

Prerequisites: familiarity with the Godot editor, scenes, and nodes. The examples introduce the Odin syntax and networking concepts they use.
